# Research prompt

Drives discovery — the part that goes looking for what the feeds did not carry.
**This file is yours. Edit it freely.**

Each `kind: discovery` source in `config/sources.yaml` names one sweep area in
its `tags`; this file says what a good find looks like in any of them. Adding a
sweep area is a `sources.yaml` edit plus a heading here.

Discovery returns **candidate URLs only**. It never summarises: the pipeline
fetches, extracts and reads each page itself, so anything asserted here would be
a summary of a summary and could not be grounded.

---

## Sweep areas

### Sweep: frontier labs & model releases — **weight this heaviest**
OpenAI (GPT-5.x/ChatGPT), Anthropic (Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku/Fable), Google
DeepMind (Gemini 3 line), xAI (Grok), Meta (Llama 4, Meta Superintelligence
Labs), and the Chinese frontier tier when it's genuinely competing at the top
of a leaderboard. Version releases, system-card disclosures, benchmark claims
(SWE-bench, GPQA, ARC-AGI, LMArena Elo movement), and named capability jumps.
This is the pipeline's anchor desk — everything else in the domain is read
against who currently holds the capability lead, so a marginal item here beats
a strong item anywhere else.

Include **counter-signals**: benchmark contamination or gaming claims,
independent evals that contradict a lab's own numbers, releases that land flat
against hype, or credible arguments that scaling gains are flattening. Evidence
the race is slowing or the gains are cosmetic is worth more than another
incremental leaderboard screenshot.

### Sweep: compute, chips & infrastructure
Nvidia's Blackwell-to-Rubin transition, TSMC CoWoS packaging capacity, HBM
(HBM3e/HBM4) supply constraints, hyperscaler capex disclosures (Microsoft,
Google, Amazon, Meta), data-center buildout including Stargate-scale projects,
and custom silicon (TPU/Ironwood, Trainium, Broadcom-designed ASICs, AMD
Instinct). This is the layer that sets the industry's pace as much as model
releases do, and it's reported mostly by specialist semiconductor and
financial press that general AI feeds don't carry — which is exactly why it
needs its own sweep rather than incidental pickup.

### Sweep: AI safety, security & alignment
Interpretability research, red-teaming results, updates to a lab's own
scaling policy (Anthropic's RSP, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, Google
DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework), third-party model evaluations (METR,
Apollo Research, UK AI Security Institute, US CAISI), disclosed scheming or
deceptive-alignment findings, and reported agentic-AI incidents in the wild.
Distinct publishers and cadence from product-release coverage — a lab's own
announcement of a capability is not the same story as an independent group's
evaluation of it.

### Sweep: policy, regulation & geopolitics
EU AI Act enforcement actions (high-risk obligations are now live), US state
AI law (California SB 53 and peers), US-China chip export controls, CAC
generative-AI service approvals, the AI safety summit track, and sovereign-AI
programs (Gulf compute deals, national model initiatives). A binding-regulation
story outranks a proposed-regulation story; an enforcement action outranks a
statement of intent.

### Sweep: enterprise adoption, agents & applications
Coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot) and computer-use
agents moving into production, enterprise deployment numbers, named platform
releases (Microsoft Copilot/Foundry, Salesforce Agentforce, Palantir AIP),
vertical deployments (healthcare, legal, finance), and agent-security incidents
(prompt injection, unsanctioned agent actions, data exposure). This is where
model capability turns into revenue and risk, and it's undercovered by feeds
that only track research and lab news.

### Sweep: funding, deals & corporate strategy
VC mega-rounds and valuation marks, compute-supply and cloud partnerships
(the OpenAI-Microsoft-Nvidia-AMD-Oracle web, Anthropic-Google-Amazon), M&A and
acquihires, IPO speculation (CoreWeave-adjacent names, Cerebras and peers),
and the running capex-bubble debate among analysts. Business press territory,
not lab or research feeds — a specific term sheet or disclosed valuation beats
another "sources say a round is coming" rumor.

### Sweep: open source & research ecosystem
Open-weight releases (Llama, Mistral, gpt-oss), the Chinese open-weight tier
(DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM), arXiv papers with real traction, Hugging Face
leaderboard movement, NeurIPS/ICML acceptances and results, and fine-tuning
technique papers (DPO, GRPO, LoRA-family methods). Moves on its own schedule,
increasingly led out of China, and needs dedicated discovery beyond arXiv's
own noisy firehose.

### Sweep: talent & org dynamics
Named researcher departures and hires, lab spin-outs (Safe Superintelligence,
Thinking Machines Lab, and their successors), leadership shakeups,
compensation-war disclosures (comp packages, poaching offers), and internal
restructurings. A recurring leading indicator of where frontier capability is
migrating, and it's broken by scoop-driven outlets, not official channels — so
official blogs will almost never carry this sweep's best finds.

### Sweep: robotics & embodied AI
Humanoid robot programs (Figure, Tesla Optimus, 1X NEO), Boston Dynamics,
world-model and robot-foundation-model research, and embodied-AI funding
rounds. A genuinely contested desk versus a subset of Enterprise Applications
— it needs its own sweep because incidental pickup from the enterprise sweep
keeps missing it.

---

## What counts as a find

A **specific, attributable development**: a model release with a version
number, a benchmark result with a source, a disclosed funding figure, a named
departure, a filed regulation, a signed compute deal.

Prefer the item with a number, a name and a date attached over the item with a
theme. *"Anthropic shipped Claude Opus 5.1 on Aug 29, reporting a 6-point jump
on SWE-bench Verified over Opus 5"* is a find. *"AI models keep getting
better at coding"* is not.

## Recency

**A page older than 48 hours is discarded before anyone reads it.** Not
deprioritised — dropped, by publication date, after the page is fetched. So an
older result is not a weaker answer, it is a wasted slot.

Prioritise the **last 24 hours**; 48 is the hard edge.

This paragraph used to say older material "is filtered out downstream", which
was true only at the brief — after the fetch, the extraction and a scoring call
had all been paid for. It is enforced at fetch now, so the instruction and the
behaviour finally agree.

Two consequences worth stating plainly, because they run against the instinct to
return a full list:

- **Returning three recent items beats returning eight where five are old.** The
  slots are not a quota.
- **A theme with nothing new is a real answer.** Return nothing for it. A quiet
  sweep is not a failed sweep, and reaching further back to fill the list is
  precisely the failure — the older pages that rank well are usually ones our
  own RSS feeds already carried, which means the slot bought nothing at all.

## Sources worth reaching for

TechCrunch, Ars Technica, VentureBeat, MIT Technology Review, WIRED, The
Information, 404 Media, Platformer, SemiAnalysis (compute/chips), Bloomberg
and Reuters tech desks, official lab channels (OpenAI News, Anthropic News,
Google DeepMind Blog, NVIDIA Newsroom, Mistral AI News, Meta AI Blog),
Hugging Face Blog and Daily Papers, arXiv cs.AI, and insider newsletters
(Import AI, Interconnects, The Batch, Don't Worry About the Vase).

A hint about where the news lives, not a whitelist. A good find on a site not
listed here is still a good find. Prefer primary sources — a lab's own
announcement, a system card, a filed regulation, a company press release —
over aggregators repeating them.

## Do not return

- **Pure geopolitics.** General US-China tension or diplomatic coverage
  belongs here only when it directly drives a chip export rule, an approval
  decision, or another concrete AI-industry consequence.
- **Opinion columns and think-pieces.** Analysis of a real development is
  fine; a columnist's take on "what AGI means" is not itself a development.
- **Vendor marketing.** A release announcing a real model, benchmark result or
  funding round is a find; a blog post about "the future of AI-powered
  productivity" is not.
- **Market-research-report spam.** "The global AI market will reach $X
  trillion by 2030" is never a find.
- **A restatement of something already widely covered**, unless it adds a
  fact — a new number, a new name, a new date.
- **Anything you cannot point at a real URL for.** No inferred links, no
  reconstructed URLs, no "this is probably at".
